newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW-Mexico vote may mean tough negotiations.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Mexico vote may mean tough negotiations.

text.p: The chance that Mexico's ruling party may lose its majority in July's Congressional elections would mean tough negotiations on issues including the budget, Deputy Finance Minister Martin Werner said.
Mexico votes for a new lower house and a quarter of the Senate on July 6. Polls show the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) may lose its lower house majority for the first time ever.

But in an interview with Reuters late Wednesday, Werner said he was confident the new Congress would be workable, whatever its composition, and said a government program for growth launched Tuesday would be an important negotiating tool.
"In the scenario of a more pluralistic Congress, we feel that it's probably going to require more negotiation to get the budget approved," he said.
"We will have to work harder to get things agreed, but in the long run we see no problem in moving along with the economic program, even in a more pluralistic environment," Werner added.

He was speaking a day after President Ernesto Zedillo presented an upbeat plan designed to guarantee five percent annual growth and create a million jobs each year until 2000, when Zedillo's six-year term ends.
The National Program for Financing Development was launched just a month before the elections, when Mexicans will also vote for six state governors and the first-ever elected mayor of the capital.

But Werner said the prospect of Mexico undergoing a period of French-style "co-habitation" would not pose any significant policy hurdles. France has just announced the formation of a new left-wing coalition under the conservative presidency of Jacques Chirac.
"Many countries in the world have a difference between an executive of one party and a more pluralistic Congress...and they manage, and I see no problem with us managing," he said.
He dismissed criticisms that the plan, which promises 7.5 percent inflation, 5.6 percent economic growth and an increase in domestic savings by the 2000 election year, was a mid-term election ploy.

"On the contrary, in light maybe of a more pluralistic Congress in the next few years, having this programme in place will be a very useful tool for discussions on economic policy in Congress," he said.

Recent opinion polls show the left-wing opposition Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) starting to make incursions into the PRI's vote. The PRD is also gaining at the expense of the more market-friendly National Action Party (PAN).
Government sources said Tuesday's economic plan was partly intended to "raise the political cost" for any opposition party trying to change economic policy after July's vote.

"If we present a plan that leads everyone to expect fiscal responsibility, low inflation and steady growth in coming years, anyone who wants to do things differently will have to explain themselves," a source said.
The prospect of gains by the PRD, which opposes the PRI on everything from private pensions to renegotiating Mexico's debt, is starting to worry investors nervous of backsliding on economic reform.
Werner said the PRD blew hot and cold on matters like the formation now underway of private pension funds.

"The PRD (last week) recommended workers not to join (funds), but on other occasions and with other audiences, especially when they go to New York or Washington, members of the PRD have said...that they realise the importance of domestic savings, which is contradictory," he said.
But he stressed that cooperating with opposition parties would be a working reality.
"We've worked with Congress in the past, and we'll have to work harder in the next three years, but that's going to be a fact of life in Mexico in the future," he said.
